source_text:
The town council has approved a new public library on the former bus depot site beside the river. The decision followed a public meeting on 6 May. Construction will start in June, and the building will open on 18 March next year. The council said the library would remain free to enter. The project includes a reading garden, a classroom, a children's room and a quiet study floor. It replaces a small library in the town hall, which will stay open until the move is complete. Staff said there would be no gap in the lending service.

The approved building has two floors and a step-free entrance facing the market square. The main desk, children's shelves and classroom will be on the ground floor. The upper floor will hold reference books, desks and quiet reading seats. A lift and a staircase will connect the floors. Large windows will face the garden, while shaded windows on the river side will reduce afternoon heat. The plans keep the old depot clock above the entrance. A local workshop will repair the clock before it is put back in place.

The council has set aside money from its existing building fund for the project. It has not announced an increase in local taxes to pay for the library. A separate reserve covers the removal of the depot's damaged roof and the repair of a retaining wall. Council officers will publish spending reports at each stage of construction. These reports will distinguish the original building work from any later change. The project team must explain a change before spending the reserve. Furniture and book purchases have their own budget and will not be charged to the construction reserve.

The contractor will put up a fence in June and clear the site before foundation work begins. Heavy deliveries will use the road behind the depot rather than the market square. Deliveries are not permitted during the weekly Saturday market. A signed walking route will keep access to the riverside path open throughout construction. The team will publish a notice before any short path closure needed for a delivery. Nearby shops will receive the same notice. A named project telephone line will accept questions during working hours, and staff will post written answers to common questions at the town hall.

Library staff asked residents what the new building should provide during three public sessions in February. Families asked for space where children could read aloud without disturbing quiet study. Students asked for evening opening and desks with power sockets. Older residents asked for clear signs, comfortable seats and help with online forms. The final plan gives the children's room its own door and places quiet study on the upper floor. The classroom can be used without opening the whole library. Staff said these choices came from the sessions, not from a survey of visitors to the current building alone.

The new library will keep the town's existing lending rules. Residents can borrow books with a free library card, and visitors can read newspapers and reference material without a card. There will be no charge for using a study desk. Printing will keep the current published charge per page. The council has not approved a cafe or a shop inside the building. A drinking-water point and seats for people waiting for an event will be near the entrance. The garden will be open during library hours and will not have a separate admission fee or booking system.

The children's room will have low shelves, movable seats and space for group reading. Its weekly story session will continue on Wednesday mornings. Schools can book the classroom for visits, but ordinary readers will not need to book a place in the children's room. Staff will move the existing children's collection before ordering new books. Teachers have been asked to suggest books that support reading for pleasure rather than school examinations alone. The council said the room would not be used as a substitute classroom during normal school hours, and the library would not take responsibility for unsupervised school groups.

The study floor will provide forty desks, including twelve that can be reserved for short group projects. The remaining desks will be available on arrival. Group work will be limited to a room with a closing door so that the rest of the floor stays quiet. Staff will publish the reservation rules before opening. The library will also provide six computers for public use. People can ask for help with a computer at the main desk. The service will not store copies of personal documents left on those computers after a session, and users will be reminded to sign out.

The reading garden will use the strip of land between the library and the riverside path. Its planting plan includes fruit trees, low flowering plants and a sheltered bench. A rainwater tank will supply the garden during dry periods. The garden club has offered to help with seasonal planting, but routine maintenance will remain the council's responsibility. The project does not include work on the river bank. The existing flood barrier will stay in place, and the library entrance will sit above the level required by the town's current building rules. Officers said the garden must not narrow the public path.

The old library will close for two days in March while staff move the final books and test the lending equipment. Readers will be able to return books through the town hall's return slot during those two days. Loan periods that end during the move will be extended without a charge. The council will announce the exact closure dates after the building inspection. The building cannot open to readers until that inspection is complete. A public walk-through will be offered after the inspection, with separate times for families, school staff and residents who want to see the study floor.

The project team plans to publish a construction update each month. Each update will state which work has finished, what is next and whether the opening date has changed. Photographs will show the building rather than identifiable visitors. The council's library committee will review the updates at its ordinary meetings. If weather or supply delays change the schedule, the team must state the effect on the opening date instead of reporting only the percentage of work complete. Staff said the updates would remain available at the town hall for residents who do not use the internet.

At the end of the meeting, the council confirmed the final opening arrangements. The new library will open on 18 March next year. For its first six weeks, it will also open late on Thursdays for free evening reading sessions. These sessions need no ticket or booking and will include access to the garden when weather permits. The first Thursday session will focus on stories about the river and the town. Staff will review attendance after six weeks before deciding whether late Thursday opening should continue. This trial does not change the normal Wednesday children's story session.
reference_summary_text: The council approved a free public library on the former riverside bus depot site. Construction starts in June and the library opens on 18 March next year. It will include a reading garden, classroom, children's room and forty study desks. The old library will stay open until the move, with a two-day closure and extended loans. Free late Thursday reading sessions will run for the first six weeks without tickets or bookings.
